summary: Intro demo covering API parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood, high-level Console walkthrough (routes, model pins, rollouts), and Optimize recommendations (batching, quantization). Discussed security (VPC/private deployment, SOC2, KMS), cost/latency tradeoffs, and pilot next steps.
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, welcome, um this is Lena from Redwood - I'm the AE on this account. We have Omar from solutions engineering as well. Quick intros?
[00:06] Maya Chen: Hi I'm Maya, CTO at Horizon Analytics, thanks for doing this, we've been evaluating OpenAI and Anthropic, and also looked at TogetherAI, we're mostly focused on migration patterns and parity.
[00:14] Ben Torres: Hey Ben here, engineering lead, I'll be doing the integration.
[00:17] Arun Patel: Arun, security/compliance.
[00:19] Zoe Li: Zoe, ML engineering, will run the evals.
[00:21] Paul: Paul in procurement, will be on later parts.
[00:23] Lena Park: Great, thanks. Quick runbook for the demo — we'll do a short parity walkthrough (OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood API), then show the Console for routing and rollouts, and end with Optimize recommendations and next steps, ok?
[00:33] Maya Chen: Sounds good.
[00:36] Omar Singh: Cool, I'll share my screen, give me a sec.
[00:40] [screen share begins]
[00:42] Omar Singh: Alright, so first, API parity. The Redwood REST surface is intentionally similar to the popular provider APIs: you have a /v1/generate and /v1/chat endpoints, embeddings endpoint, and streaming via chunked transfer; function-calling is supported via structured JSON.
[00:58] Zoe Li: Is the streaming format identical to OpenAI? We use delta tokens heavily.
[01:02] Omar Singh: It's close — we stream chunked JSON with delta tokens. Slight differences: our event names are `chunk` and `done` in the stream, some clients need a tiny mapping layer but most SDKs handle it. There are known differences for Anthropic-style token framing, we include an adapter in our SDKs.
[01:20] Ben Torres: How about function calling? We rely on that for tool orchestration.
[01:23] Omar Singh: Supported — schema-based function calling works, we map OpenAI function schema to Redwood's `tools` payload. Example snippet I showed in the docs — same semantics, small field name changes (OpenAI `name`/`arguments` -> Redwood `id`/`params`), we provide example mapping scripts.
[01:39] Maya Chen: Great. One of our concerns is hallucination differences between Anthropic and OpenAI outputs — can Redwood control temperature/penalty knobs the same way?
[01:47] Omar Singh: Yes, all the usual hyperparameters (temperature, top_p, presence/ frequency penalties) are exposed. We also expose model variants with calibrated temperature defaults for safety; Optimize can suggest a profile that balances quality vs token cost.
[02:00] Lena Park: Quick question on embeddings — we currently use OpenAI text-embedding-3-small for semantic search. If we move to Redwood with an open model, how disruptive is the vector format and similarity scoring?
[02:10] Omar Singh: We keep standard float32 arrays and support cosine/inner product L2 norms. If you change model families, there is reindexing cost — but Redwood Optimize can recommend a migration strategy: small A/B index, re-embed cold data on demand, or use hybrid matching. We also support dense+quantized vectors for lower storage.
[02:30] Zoe Li: You said quantized vectors — are they still compatible with FAISS and our current vector DB?
[02:34] Omar Singh: Yes, we export standard flat or IVF indexes and provide export tools. Quantization for inference is handled in the runtime only; we don't force a proprietary vector format.
[02:45] [03:00] Ben Torres: On the Console, can you show model pins and rollout? We want canary to 5% and auto fallback to hosted smaller model on latency spikes.
[03:08] Omar Singh: Absolutely — switching to Console view — here we have a route configured for /api/generate pointing at `redwood-gpt-large`. Rollout tab lets you define canary, percentage, and auto-fallback rules (e.g., latency > 800ms for 1 minute -> fallback to `gpt-medium-quant`). You can also set model-specific rate limits and cost caps.
[03:29] Maya Chen: Nice. Is the fallback instantaneous if GPU pool is saturated?
[03:33] Omar Singh: Practically yes, routing is at the request layer — we check policy and route to hot spare model variants. There is a tiny switch but typically sub-second.
[03:40] Arun Patel: Let's talk security — VPC/private deployment options and key management. We are in finance so need KMS + audit logs.
[03:47] Lena Park: Redwood Private supports VPC deployments and on-prem if needed; keys can be customer-managed in KMS/HSM and audit logs exported to your SIEM. We have SOC 2 Type II; I'll attach the security pack.
[04:00] Arun Patel: Do you support SSO/SAML and RBAC scoped to model routes?
[04:04] Omar Singh: Yes SSO via SAML/OIDC, and fine-grained RBAC — you can restrict who can change rollout policies or access keys. Audit trail shows user, action, timestamp.
[04:14] Maya Chen: Data residency? We have EU-only requirements for some PII.
[04:18] Lena Park: You can pin deployments to region — Redwood's hosted offering has EU regions; for strict residency we recommend Private VPC or on-prem bundle.
[04:26] Paul: On cost — approximate savings we might see moving off OpenAI?
[04:29] Omar Singh: It depends on model/quantization. For many workloads switching to curated open models + 4-bit quantization and batching gives 2–5x token cost reduction; Optimize's suggestions show specific numbers based on your token distribution.
[04:43] Ben Torres: Can you walk through a parity mapping example — a concrete request from OpenAI and Redwood equivalent?
[04:49] Omar Singh: Sure, here's a quick side-by-side — OpenAI `POST /v1/chat/completions` with messages -> Redwood `POST /v1/chat` with `input` array. Stream mapping slightly different but we included an adapter. I'll paste an example in chat.
[05:05] [Omar pastes example link in chat: https://redwood.example/docs/parity-mapping]
[05:09] Zoe Li: Ok will review. How are you handling Anthropic-style prompts? We have a few safety wrappers using Anthropic system prompts.
[05:16] Omar Singh: Anthropic's prompt style is supported via compatibility mode — we translate the `system`/`assistant` prefixes to Redwood-structured messages. In some cases you may need to tweak a few tokens for identical outputs; Optimize's eval runs can measure delta against baseline and suggest small prompt changes or post-processing to align outputs.
[05:35] Maya Chen: About latency — we have a p95 SLA of 600ms for interactive chat. Can you reach that on Redwood hosted?
[05:43] Omar Singh: For typical seq len <= 512 we can meet p95 ~200–400ms on dedicated pools. Hosted is more variable; Dedicated reserved GPU capacity will give you predictable latency and Redwood Dedicated comes with SLA targets.
[05:58] Ben Torres: If we do a pilot, how long to get a dedicated tenant?
[06:02] Lena Park: For pilot we usually start on hosted with reserved capacity for your account; a Dedicated provision (private GPU pool) typically takes a few weeks depending on contract. We can do a 30-day pilot on hosted with near-dedicated guarantees.
[06:14] Arun Patel: For the pilot we need a configuration that ensures data isn't used for model training and has log forwarding to our SIEM.
[06:21] Lena Park: We have a controls package for pilots: no-training pledge for your tenant, KMS for encryption, and audit/export hooks. We'll share the compliance doc.
[06:31] Zoe Li: Going back to runtimes — what's the KV cache story; we have long conversation context and would like prefix cache.
[06:37] Omar Singh: KV cache is supported — prefix caching, token-aware invalidation, and shared caches across sessions for identical prefixes. Optimize can recommend cache TTLs based on hit rates. There's also continuous batching that pairs nicely with prefix cache to reduce GPU ops.
[06:52] Ben Torres: Any gotchas moving from TogetherAI? They have a different streaming loop.
[06:57] Omar Singh: Together's streaming loop semantics differ a bit; we included example adapters and a mapping layer in our SDKs. In our experience the mapping is small; most engineering time is in validating prompts and running acceptance tests.
[07:10] Maya Chen: For embeddings drift — if we re-embed everything with a different model, search results may change. Do you have tooling to compare old vs new?
[07:18] Omar Singh: Yes, Optimize includes a reranking evaluation harness — run topic-based QA sets and compute recall/ndcg deltas. We can also do hybrid indexes so you only reembed top-k cold docs.
[07:33] Lena Park: I want to show the Optimize suggestions tab — gives recommended batch sizes, quantization profile, and expected cost delta.
[07:40] [Omar switches to Optimize tab]
[07:43] Omar Singh: Here we ingested a synthetic traffic profile and it recommends: for your distribution (p95 length ~620) — use model `rwd-gpt-3.5-q4` for general chat with batch size 8 and enable KV prefix cache TTL 30s; estimated cost 2.3x lower than cloud baseline.
[07:58] Zoe Li: p95 620 is larger than we thought — that's from our analytics, yes. Would batch size 8 increase latency?
[08:03] Omar Singh: Batching trades latency for throughput, Optimize recommends targeting 90th percentile latency within SLO; for interactive flows we set smaller batch sizes or dedicated warm pools.
[08:12] Ben Torres: Show me the observability — token-level cost and tracing.
[08:15] Omar Singh: Console trace for a sample request — shows token timing breakdown (prefix load, KV hit, decode), model used, cost estimate, and a waterfall chart. You can set alerts if token cost per request spikes.
[08:30] Maya Chen: A couple of quick clarifying Qs — will we have to change our webhooks? Also what about rate limits?
[08:36] Omar Singh: Webhooks for async responses are supported; if you use OpenAI webhooks there is a simple mapping. Rate limits are configurable per route; we can mirror your existing limits during migration.
[08:47] Paul: Procurement note — if we go to Dedicated, what's the billing cadence and commitment?
[08:52] Lena Park: Dedicated is typically monthly or annual commits. We can provide an estimate for your expected consumption and propose a reserved capacity contract with burst credits. We'll include sample SOW in the follow-up.
[09:04] Maya Chen: Great. Walk me through a sample curl migration for a chat request?
[09:07] Omar Singh: Sure — small live demo: OpenAI curl vs Redwood curl.
[09:10] [Omar types example]
[09:14] Omar Singh: OpenAI: curl -X POST https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions -d '{"model":"gpt-4o","messages":[...]}'
[09:22] Omar Singh: Redwood: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' -d '{"model":"redwood-gpt-large","input":[{"role":"system","content":"..."},{"role":"user","content":"..."}] }'
[09:41] Zoe Li: Will the tokens count change significantly?
[09:44] Omar Singh: Different tokenizers can cause small deltas; Optimize reports per-request token mapping and suggests detokenization steps if you need exact parity.
[09:55] Maya Chen: For our pilot timeline — we want a 2-week technical validation and a 4-week pilot with sample production traffic. Feels feasible?
[10:03] Lena Park: Yes, typical flow: week 0 — parity mapping & smoke tests; week 1 — start benchmark & acceptance tests; weeks 2–5 — pilot with controlled traffic; we support cockpit monitoring.
[10:12] Ben Torres: How much engineering effort should we budget? 
[10:15] Omar Singh: From other customers, mapping + integration + acceptance tests are usually 1–2 SRE/ML engineer-weeks for chat+embeddings if adapters are used.
[10:24] Arun Patel: Security review usually is the blocker — we'll send our list.
[10:28] Lena Park: Understood — we'll prioritize the compliance pack and SOC 2 artifacts.
[10:33] Maya Chen: Any limitations on model types e.g., LLaMA-family or closed weights?
[10:38] Omar Singh: We support a curated catalog, including LLaMA-style open weights and some licensed proprietary variants; private deployments can accept customer-provided models if licensing allows.
[10:48] Zoe Li: Quick question — how do you handle model rollbacks? If a rollout causes regression, can we auto rollback?
[10:54] Omar Singh: Yes, rollout policies include automatic rollback triggers (quality/regression alerts, latency spikes, error %); you can tie those to A/B evaluation metrics.
[11:03] Ben Torres: Show us the logfile export for a failing request.
[11:06] Omar Singh: Here — trace includes request payload, model id, token timing, and raw model output. We can redact PII and forward to your SIEM.
[11:18] [11:30] Maya Chen: This has been super helpful. A couple more housekeeping items: we'll need pricing for pilot, security docs, and a parity mapping example— those are the main deliverables.
[11:39] Lena Park: That's exactly what we'll send. Quick recap and owners: Lena will send pricing and security pack; Omar will run benchmark and share mappings; Maya/Zoe will provide sample prompts and traffic. We'll aim to have those items out by end of next day.
[11:53] Paul: From procurement side we'll need a draft SOW and T&Cs.
[11:56] Lena Park: Roger that, we'll include a pilot SOW template.
[12:00] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone.
[12:02] Lena Park: Thanks, talk soon.
[12:05] [call ends]
